question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 16$ between the surfaces $z = 0$ and $z = \sqrt{25 - (x^2 + y^2)}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R z \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $4$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = \sqrt{25 - (x^2 + y^2)} = \sqrt{25 - r^2}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 4, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{25-r^2} \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R z \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta z r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] %& = \iiint\limits_\Delta r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\sqrt{25-r^2} }} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} rz} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=25$ for $x \geq 0$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=6+y.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R xz \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $5$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=6+y = 6 + r\sin\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 5, \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 6+r\sin\theta \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R xz \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta (r\cos\theta)z \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-\pi/2}}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{5} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}6+r\sin\theta}} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r^2 z \cos\theta} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ for $x \geq 0$ and $y \geq 0,$ between the surfaces $z = 1$ and $z = x^2 + y^2 + 4.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 2xy \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-quarter of a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{2}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z = 1,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = x^2 + y^2 + 4 = r^2 + 4.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{2}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 1 \leq z \leq r^2 + 4 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R 2xy \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta 2(r\cos{\theta})(r\sin{\theta}) \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi/2}} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} \int_{1}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}r^2+4 }} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r^3\sin{2\theta}} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

  • bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = \sqrt{16 - (x^2 + y^2)} = \sqrt{16 - r^2}.$

question.text: If the solid region $R$ is given by \[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 + (y+3)^2 \leq 9, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2+x^2+y^2 \right\}, \] then $\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R xy \: \textrm{d}V =$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,-3)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=2+x^2+y^2 = 2+r^2.$

With that in mind, let's write the equation $x^2 + (y+3)^2 = 9$ in polar coordinates:

\begin{align*} x^2 + (y+3)^2 & = 9 \\[5pt] \left(r\cos{\theta}\right)^2 + \left(r\sin{\theta} +3\right)^2 & = 9 \\[5pt] r^2\cos^2{\theta} + r^2\sin^2{\theta} + 6r\sin{\theta} + 9 & = 9 \\[5pt] r^2(\cos^2{\theta} + \sin^2{\theta}) + 6r\sin{\theta} &= 0 \\[5pt] r^2 + 6r\sin{\theta} & = 0\\[5pt] r(r + 6\sin{\theta}) & = 0 \end{align*}

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = -6\sin{\theta}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq -6\sin\theta, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2+r^2 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R xy \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta (r\cos\theta)(r\sin\theta) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-6\sin\theta}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2+r^2}} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r^3 \cos\theta \sin\theta} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

question.text: If the solid region $R$ is given by \[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, (x-2)^2 + y^2 \leq 4, \: y-4 \leq z \leq 3 \right\}, \] then $\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R z \: \textrm{d}V =$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(2,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z = y-4 = r\sin{\theta}-4,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = 3.$

With that in mind, let's write the equation $(x-2)^2 + y^2 = 4$ in polar coordinates: \begin{align*} (x-2)^2 + y^2 & = 4 \\[5pt] \left(r\cos{\theta} - 2\right)^2 + \left(r\sin{\theta}\right)^2 & = 4 \\[5pt] r^2\cos^2{\theta} - 4r\cos{\theta} + 4 + r^2\sin^2{\theta} & = 4 \\[5pt] r^2(\cos^2{\theta} + \sin^2{\theta}) - 4r\cos{\theta} & = 0 \\[5pt] r^2 - 4r\cos{\theta} & = 0\\[5pt] r(r - 4\cos{\theta}) & = 0 \end{align*}

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = 4\cos{\theta}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 4\cos{\theta}, \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin{\theta}-4 \leq z \leq 3 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R z \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta z r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4\cos\theta}} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}r\sin{\theta}-4}}^{3} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} rz } \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq -4\sin{\theta}, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: -r\sin{\theta}-3 \leq z \leq 3 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 + 1 \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \left( \left(r\cos{\theta})^2+(r\sin{\theta}\right)^2 + 1 \right) \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] % & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \left( r^2\cos^2{\theta}+r^2\sin^2{\theta} + 1 \right) \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \left( r^2\left(\cos^2{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}\right) + 1 \right) \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi}}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{-4\sin{\theta}} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-r\sin{\theta}-3}}^{3} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r(r^2 + 1) } \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=9$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{9-(x^2-y^2)}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=\sqrt{9-(x^2-y^2)} =\sqrt{9-r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)}=\sqrt{9-r^2\cos(2\theta)}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{9-r^2\cos(2\theta) }\right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin\theta}} \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{3} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{9-r^2\cos(2\theta)}} z \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{3} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}z^2\right]_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{9-r^2\cos(2\theta)}} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{9-r^2\cos(2\theta)}\right)^2 \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{1}{2}\left(9-r^2\cos(2\theta)\right) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{9}{2}r - \dfrac{1}{6}r^3\cos(2\theta) \right]_{r=0}^{r=3} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{9}{2}(3)- \dfrac{1}{6}(3)^3\cos(2\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{27}{2}- \dfrac{9}{2}\cos(2\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{27}{2}\theta -\dfrac{9}{4}\sin(2\theta) \right]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{27}{2}(2\pi- 0) - \dfrac{9}{4}(0-0) \\[5pt] &= 27\pi. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=3$ for $x\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+4.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{3}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=y=r\sin\theta,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=y+4 =r\sin\theta + 4.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{3}, \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin\theta \leq z \leq r \sin\theta +4 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta r\cos\theta\sqrt{(r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2} \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} \int_{r\sin\theta}^{r\sin\theta+4} r^3\cos\theta \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} r^3\cos\theta \big[ z \big]_{z=r\sin\theta}^{z=r\sin\theta+4} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} r^3\cos\theta (r\sin\theta+4-r\sin\theta) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}} 4r^3\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \big[ r^4 \cos\theta \big]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sqrt{3})^4\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 9\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \big[ 9\sin\theta \big]_{\theta=-\pi/2}^{\theta=\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= 9(1- (-1)) \\[5pt] &= 18. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2 \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=4-x.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=4-x =4-r\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 4- r \cos\theta \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2\: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \left(\left(r\cos\theta\right)^2+\left(r\sin\theta\right)^2\right)\: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{4- r\cos\theta} r^3 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r^3 \big[ z \big]_{z=0}^{z=4-r\cos\theta} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r^3 (4-r \cos\theta) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} 4r^3 - r^4 \cos\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[ r^4 - \dfrac{1}{5}r^5 \cos\theta \right]_{r=0}^{r=1} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} 1 - \dfrac{1}{5}\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \big[ \theta - \dfrac{1}{5}\sin\theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \\[5pt] &= (2\pi-0) - \dfrac{1}{5}(0-0) \\[5pt] &=2\pi. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 2z \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=9$ for $y \geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=-x$ and $z=2+x.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=-x = -r\cos\theta,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=2+x = 2 + r\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, \: -r\cos\theta \leq z \leq 2+r\cos\theta \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R 2z \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta 2z \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{3} \int_{-r\cos\theta}^{2+r\cos\theta} 2rz \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{3} r \big[ z^2 \big]_{z=-r\cos\theta}^{z=2+r\cos\theta} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{3} r \big( (2+r\cos\theta)^2 - (-r\cos\theta)^2 \big) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{3} 4r+4r^2\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \left[ 2r^2+\dfrac{4}{3}r^3 \cos\theta \right]_{r=0}^{r=3} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} 2(3)^2+\dfrac{4}{3}(3)^3 \cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} 18+36 \cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \big[ 18\theta+36 \sin\theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=\pi} \\[5pt] &= 18(\pi-0)+36(0-0) \\[5pt] &= 18\pi. \end{align*}
